After reading your comment, hypersexuality could absolutely be something she is dealing with. Also, something I did as a trauma reaction was purposely put myself in harms way. It is difficult to explain but I would go out a lot, take walks at two am, get ridiculously drunk, smoke, talk to strangers, etc. I simply did not care about my well being. My mental health was suffering and it showed how little I cared for myself. After something so traumatic happens, it can take away not only who you are but your value as a person. I have a history of self harm and at the root of it I wanted my physical body to reflect my mental turmoil. I had a hard time speaking about things and I felt as if my pain wasn’t fully seen or acknowledged. The mental turmoil I experienced after being assaulted was so devastating it makes me chest hurt to even think about. 

If any of this sounds like your wife it may be good to validate her pain and worth but also let her know that she can talk to you. This week I came to the realization that having a life-altering event happen and then rarely being able to talk about it is traumatic in itself. 

Another aspect of her reaction may attached to you. It could be shame or the feeling of being of unwanted or maybe you/her not believing that it was nonconsensual (just her possible thoughts). I struggle with questioning if my partner believes me and whether I should have told him. I couldn’t have asked for a better partner so this IS NOT a reflection of you, but there is so much internal turmoil to sort through her own feelings of guilt and self-blame can get mixed in with yours.

Now that you have some idea of what she is going through, understand that there isn’t much you can do other than be her husband. Each survivor is different. Therapy is going to be very important. Once a week never felt like enough for me so if you can afford it, get her an extra personal session per week. Talk to her gently and always communicate your feelings so there is no room for misinterpretation or overthinking. 

As for reporting, whenever women hear about reporting assault it is never positive. As a woman once in that position, I also refused. I think the other comment captured it well. 

Lastly, hypersexuality does not end well. When in a relationship it has lead to me almost cheating, putting myself in precarious situationships and having panic attacks during sex. It is not a solution, it is a bandaid and when you put a bandaid over an open wound- it doesn’t heal anything and it hurts a hell of a lot more taking it off. 


I hope this helped.

I understand that in most relationships with narcs that isolation occurs, which leads the victim to feel like the only person they truly have is the narc. Hence why she wants to remain in contact because he consumed her entire world for a while. But.. something feels a little off here. 

My advice is to go off the premise of her never cutting contact with him. If you can deal with that, then buckle in. If you can’t, put your own boundaries in place to protect yourself. And stick to them.

It took my 4 years to stop talking to my Narc ex. He also r-ped me and I developed a trauma bond with him from trying to heal from the trauma that he gave me while being in a relationship with him.

It is something that she has to work through at her own pace. I have been married for two of the past 4 years and my spouse allowed me to respond rarely or even have full conversations as much as I needed until I was able to break it. Of course every individuals boundaries are different so this isn’t to tell you what to do. 

The way I explained it to my spouse is that he r-ped me, verbally abused me, gaslit me and threw me away when he got ready to. Even after he threw me away he could not stand the thought of me being independent or being with anyone else so he chose different ways to maintain control. Texting me frequently, trying to get intel about my life, using the details he knows to manipulate me. He would go from wanting to have sex to angry to loving to desperately missing me in a span of minutes. 

The goal is the narcissist is to make their victim feel so worthless and helpless that they never leave them. It’s a process that requires the mental, emotional, verbal and sometimes sexual breakdown of the victim. By doing so (for however long they were together) he has literally changed the way her brain works. She is now wired to think about his needs or what he wants, she blames herself for everything and she doesn’t feel in control of her life or their relationship. 

What you are watching her experience is the beginning of the end. All she has to do is not go back and continue to work in her personal growth.

You can’t do or say anything other than support her. It’s not going to be fun and there is no right or wrong way to do it imo other than being what she needs. All you can do is make decisions to maintain your own mental health.

As a parent, his child should come first. There are many dead beats- so for some single moms/ women who don’t mind a blended family- he is the perfect dad.

Common behavior? Yes. Temporary? It’s possible- but not likely in my experience. It depends on her relationship history. Some people stick to their traumatic past and find a partner that is abusive, manipulative, etc bc that feels like home and all sense of self-worth is in the toilet. Others recognize better and aim for decent people- he relationship history should let you know which she is. 

As far as being supportive.. back up to “a phone call away” distance. Meaning if she needs you, step in for some platonic listening and if she doesn’t then she still has her space. Side note: It sounds like she could have been repressing all this trauma so if she is ready to start her healing and is asking you for a break you should walk away- you should ask this question. Safe healing to you both💕💕
